A U.S. postal worker has been charged with throwing away 300 mail-in ballots in Utah. (Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images file) WASHINGTON — An overwhelmed U.S. postal worker in Utah threw 300 mail-in ballots into a parking lot dumpster shortly before the state’s June 23 primary election in which both Democrats and Republicans were on the ballot, Justice Department officials said Tuesday. The 34-year-old mail carrier told investigators that he did not have a political agenda and that he tossed other mail when he ditched the ballots, Melissa Holyoak, U.S. attorney for the District of Utah, said. She said roughly 95% of voters do so by mail in the state, and it wasn’t clear yet whether they were able to eventually cast ballots. According to a government memo , Damon Matai Seei told investigators that he wanted to toss out advertisements to “lighten his workload” after feeling overwhelmed. “He claims he simply made a ‘poor decision’ out of ‘frustration’ and ‘laziness,’” the memo said. He didn’t intend to toss any ballots, they said. Seei is no longer with the U.S. Postal Service. He pleaded not guilty Tuesday to a charge of destruction and delay of mail. The U.S. Postal Service said in a statement that it works “tirelessly to ensure public trust in the mail and monitors to prevent any issues that may arise,” and that it closely monitors political and election mail. The agency said it was notified of a mail dumping, and referred the matter to the inspector general, “specifically charged with investigating alleged crimes” by postal service employees. “The unique status of political and election mail makes its security a top priority during every election cycle,” according to the statement, and works to “to prevent, identify and resolve any issues that might interfere with its secure and timely delivery.” Justice Department officials held a news conference in Washington to announce the charge as part of its efforts to promote “election integrity.” Federal prosecutors have made possible voter fraud — which is rare — a priority, as President Donald Trump insists without evidence that noncitizens are voting en masse and has sought to limit mail-in ballots. The Supreme Court last week refused to allow the president’s mail-in restrictions to be enforced. Trump has repeatedly made false claims that he won the 2020 election and has falsely claimed he won the popular vote in 2016, yet the Trump administration has struggled during both terms to bring cases showing evidence of significant voter fraud . That’s despite a massive effort in Trump’s second term to obtain voter registration records from states in an attempt to determine if there were any noncitizens registered. So far during the president’s second term, the Justice Department has charged 70 voter-fraud-related cases, officials said Tuesday. More than 170 million people are registered to vote in the U.S. Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said there were more cases in the works, but he didn’t provide further details or a timeline. “Under the leadership of President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, this department is committed to protecting the vote of American citizens,” he said. The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, meanwhile, is revving up a long-standing election monitoring program but putting a new emphasis on “ballot security” and staffing the effort with newly hired conservative personnel who have replaced longtime career employees, hundreds of whom have departed en masse since Trump returned to office. The Civil Rights Division’s efforts to seize voter rolls have resulted in a string of court losses — with 25 courts ruling against the federal government. Voting rights experts say isolated instances of fraud do happen, as do issues with voting machines, but not on a scale that could have changed the outcome of the 2020 presidential election, which was won by Democrat Joe Biden . But the materials that the Justice Department releases could help feed Trump’s broader narrative about elections. And with the majority of voters disapproving of Trump’s presidency and saying his policies have hurt the economy , Republicans are facing a tough midterms picture. Earlier this month, the Justice Department rolled out five voting-related cases , four of which were brought against noncitizens. Last week, the Justice Department announced that 16 individuals had been charged in election-related cases, with a news release mentioning that at least 10 of them were lawful permanent residents of the United States. The defendants were originally from Mexico, Nigeria, India, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Antigua and Barbuda, Venezuela, and Colombia. There was also a defendant from Russia: Victoria Aquilina, a 42-year-old Russian national who entered the United States as an au pair in her early 20s, was charged with casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Trump — who, until he won the 2024 election, faced federal criminal charges over his efforts to overturn his 2020 loss in the lead-up to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol — said earlier this year that Republicans should “ nationalize the voting .” Democrats, meanwhile, have launched an “unprecedented” effort to combat potential disruption of the 2026 midterm elections. Seei’s next court date is Nov. 30. His federal public defender did not immediately respond to a request for comment. item.title: Supreme Court stays out of custody dispute between California couple and surrogate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to intervene in a custody dispute between a California couple and surrogate who gave birth to a child last month with a rare and serious heart defect. Justice Elena Kagan rejected the emergency appeal from the woman, McKenna West, who had asked the justices to halt a California court order declaring the couple, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, to be the child's parents. Kagan handles emergency appeals arising from California and other states in the region. The legal battle involves a surrogacy contract Gilkar and Ahmed entered into with West, which allowed the couple to demand an abortion for a baby diagnosed with a fetal abnormality, according to court filings. West, who lives in Alaska, became pregnant with a baby boy in December. But in April, a 20-week anatomy scan showed the baby had hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a severe, life-threatening heart defect that prevents normal blood flow through the heart, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. After receiving the diagnosis, Gilkar and Ahmed requested West obtain an abortion, according to court filings. West refused and traveled to Texas, where she gave birth last month. She calls the baby Gabriel, and Gilkar and Ahmed named him Rumi. Texas bans abortions after roughly six weeks of pregnancy. Before the baby was born , the California couple asked a state court to confirm their parentage of the child. The California court agreed, recognizing Gilkar and Ahmed as his legal parents. The child underwent surgery in Texas soon after he was born after Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton intervened and secured a court order requiring the hospital to provide the baby with lifesaving medical care. Paxton has since withdrawn from the proceedings. That surgery, known as a Norwood procedure, is typically the first in a line of three surgeries required in the first years of life for babies born with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, according to the CDC. The Texas court also said the California couple, not West, is responsible for medical decisions for the boy. But West asked the Supreme Court to lift the California order that recognizes Gilkar and Ahmed as the baby boy's parents. In a filing, her lawyers claimed that the couple is attempting to halt lifesaving care for the child and warned that without relief, West will be denied the right to protect the baby's life. They wrote that under Texas law, West would likely be the child's rightful mother since she gave birth to him in Texas. But lawyers for Ahmed and Gilkar said in a Supreme Court filing that they have been ensuring the baby receives lifesaving care and "are committed to doing so for the rest of his life." "Respondents have been with their child around the clock in a hospital's pediatric intensive care unit," they said. "The child has been receiving critical medical care by his team of doctors at the consent and direction of Respondents." They said that intervention from the Supreme Court would cause chaos and confusion over medical decision-making for the baby, and rebutted West's need for emergency relief since Ahmed and Gilkar are providing the child with the medical care that she is pushing for. Adam Wolf, a lawyer for Gilkar and Ahmed, said in response to Kagan's denial, "We are truly grateful that Rumi can continue receiving the treatment he needs to survive, and that he will not be stripped away from what has been described by doctors as the excellent care of his parents. Ms. West's legal filings across three jurisdictions, state courts of appeals, and now the U.S. Supreme Court have sought to undermine Rumi's parents' right to provide him with the care he needs. Those efforts have been rejected by every single court." AUSTIN, Texas — The ICE officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin on Sunday, leaving a bullet lodged in his back, was issued a body camera but was not wearing it during the shooting, two officials with the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News. The officials said it was not clear why the officer was not wearing his body camera. Another ICE officer who was in the same vehicle was wearing a body camera, the officials said. That camera captured partial footage of the incident, but the footage does not include the moment of the shooting, the officials said. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez , 28, was shot early Sunday afternoon by an ICE officer while making deliveries as a DoorDash driver. He was taken to a hospital and, four hours after he was shot, was taken into immigration custody at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, his attorney said. The bullet remains in his back. On Tuesday, a federal judge granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. The Travis County District Attorney’s Office also sent a letter to DHS and ICE leadership requesting that Garcés Pérez be allowed to remain in the country since he is “a material witness” in their criminal investigation into the shooting. Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis shared on Tuesday evening some of the first video footage obtained by the department as part on their probe into the shooting. The videos came from an off-duty officer who captured part of the encounter between ICE and Garcés Pérez, as well as the sound of three gunshots, using his personal dash cam and cellphone. After this, the off-duty officer alerted his colleagues to the shooting, allowing Austin police to quickly respond to the scene. Davis said they are seeking the public’s help in obtaining any video evidence that can help them piece together the pursuit that preceded the shooting. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez was shot by an ICE officer while delivering food in Austin. (Courtesy Attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch) The day after he was shot, Garcés Pérez began “experiencing an inability to move his arm,” attorney Lincoln-Goldfinch said on social media. He was taken to the hospital Monday afternoon for several hours and then sent back to the detention center, she said. The DHS did not respond to requests for comment about Lincoln-Goldfinch’s statements. Earlier Monday, Garcés Pérez told a news conference via phone from detention that he was in a lot of pain and wasn’t getting the medical care he needed. Lincoln-Goldfinch alleged in a social media post that after Garcés Pérez spoke out at the news conference, guards at the detention center “forcibly took the tablet from his hands, revoked his communication privileges, and moved him out of the infirmary into an isolated room with a flat bed that cannot be adjusted like a medical bed.” He was then taken to the hospital around 5 p.m. after losing his ability to move his arm, she said. “Wilber reports that he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during that transfer,” she said in the post. Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garcés Pérez told her on Tuesday morning that doctors spoke to him about his care and gave him morphine for his pain. “We now understand that the gunshot fractured his clavicle and that he has significant swelling and is wearing a sling,” she wrote. “We still do not have clarity about the cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced.” Elizdar, right, wife of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, and attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. (Jay Janner / The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images) The attorney said Garcés Pérez was discharged from the hospital around midnight and taken back to the detention center, where he is receiving Tylenol and ibuprofen for his ongoing pain. “He remains in isolation, on a flat bed, and without the tablet he previously used to communicate,” she said. “We are asking for his communication privileges to be immediately restored and for him to be provided an appropriate medical bed and adequate medical care,” she said. “Most importantly, we are continuing to advocate for Wilber’s IMMEDIATE release.” Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, said on social media that “despite losing movement on his left side and having a bullet lodged next to his spine, ICE has forced Wilber Rafael out of the hospital and back to the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas.” He said that he and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, would visit Garcés Pérez on Wednesday, check on his condition and demand his release. A DHS spokesperson said in a statement late Sunday that Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and was in federal custody pending removal from the U.S. A senior administration official told NBC News on Monday that Garcés Pérez did not have a criminal history beyond being in the country illegally. According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garcés Pérez entered the country legally and was seeking asylum. She said Garcés Pérez had filed a change of address in immigration court, but received a notice to appear in court at the old address and never got it. Because he missed his immigration hearing, Garcés Pérez was ordered deported in absentia, according to his attorney. On Monday, Lincoln-Goldfinch shared Garcés Pérez’s account of the shooting, saying he was making a delivery when “an unmarked black truck sideswiped him.” She said he didn’t know it was ICE as the truck chased him as he tried to make a U-turn, and then “pulled him out of the car.” Previously, DHS has accused immigrants involved in shootings with ICE of using their cars as weapons while fleeing agents, without offering evidence of its claims. But it did not make the accusation in the case of Garcés Pérez or in the case of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot in Biddeford, Maine, in July during a traffic stop. ICE Director David Venturella previously told NBC News that every ICE officer and agent would be equipped with body cameras by the end of August, adding the agency would allow the “expedited release” of bodycam footage “when appropriate.” Further delaying that timeline is the possibility of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin potentially switching or adding new vendors for body cameras. A person who witnessed the aftermath of the shooting but who requested anonymity because he is going through immigration proceedings told Noticias Telemundo that he was waiting on customers at the ice cream shop where he works when he heard gunshots and ran outside, where he saw immigration agents surrounding a car. “I approached the car and saw a man who looked sad and with his eyes full of tears. I asked him what happened to him, and he just told me, ‘I was shot in the back,’” said the person, a Mexican immigrant who has lived in the U.S. for more than two decades. “You aren’t prepared to see someone like that. It makes you very angry, it pains you and you don’t know what to do,” he said. A social media video verified by NBC News captures the sound of tires screeching followed by a person exiting a dark-colored SUV as a blue sedan is stopped next to it, both vehicles facing each other. The sedan appears to be damaged on the passenger side. At least three gunshots are heard as the person approaches the sedan and runs up to it as it slowly lurches forward. The video shows the person standing next to the sedan’s driver’s side as it stops in front of an intersection. Another video shows the blue sedan with its driver’s side door open and Garcés Pérez hunched over in the driver’s seat, holding his left upper chest, near his shoulder, as multiple law enforcement officers gather around. The woman taking the video says, “Why did he do that to him?” The officers tell her that an ambulance is coming. The video shows Garcés Pérez being taken out of the car and handcuffed behind his back. The agents make him sit on the ground. There appears to be a large bloodstain down his back. The officers cut open the back of his shirt, revealing a bullet hole. An officer asks the woman taking the video if she saw what happened. In Spanish, she replies that “they just shot him because he didn’t want to stop” his vehicle. “This is unjust,” she says as she’s recording the video. item.title: Justice Department says Trump can deny journalists White House access
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Three leading US news outlets went to court after being banned from the White House by President Donald Trump (Jim WATSON) CNN, MS NOW and Politico can be shut out from areas of the White House at President Donald Trump's request, the Department of Justice said on Tuesday, a day ahead of a court hearing. The three leading outlets went to court after Trump ordered on Friday that they be barred from the presidential mansion as punishment for distributing what he calls "fake news." A US district judge set a hearing on the complaint for Wednesday. The Department of Justice said in a court filing that Trump can "control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office." "Access to the White House is a privilege -- not a right," it added. The court filing said that letters explaining the president's reasons for the ban had been sent to the outlets on Tuesday. They have until Friday to object. The letters cite numerous "reporting incidents" by the outlets that "threatened national security and spread falsehoods," according to the filing. The letter to CNN cited a story on Trump's plans to build a bunker below the East Wing ballroom he is constructing, which "disclosed 'top-secret' construction details," and several stories about the Iran war, the network said. Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied any access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated. In their lawsuit, the three outlets asked for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press. "This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the outlets said in the court filing. On Tuesday, Trump appeared to have suggested that CNN should not be covering him outside of the White House too. "I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me, you shouldn't be here," Trump told reporters covering his visit to the United Nations General Assembly this week. Trump has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people." But the ban comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows, his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections, and the war in the Middle East drags on with no end in sight. bur-lkd/ami This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-justice-dept-says-trump-074536366.html

item.title: El Niño predicted to cause nearly half a million more deaths
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
BENGALURU, India (AP) — This year's powerful El Nino and the record global heat it's driving, along with severe droughts, wildfires and shrinking water supplies, could lead to nearly half a million more deaths worldwide by the end of February, according to a research report released Wednesday. The grim warning by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab says that as many as 451,000 more heat-related deaths between June and the end of February could be attributed to El Nino, compared with heat deaths expected in a typical year. The heaviest toll, the group says, is expected in poorer countries, already struggling with food insecurity and high energy costs, partly due to climate change and the fallout of the war in Iran . Michael Greenstone, a co-founder of the group and the study's co-author, said the heat danger will likely persist beyond February — even though this El Nino is expected to end by then. The fallout of the weather phenomenon could be felt well into next summer, he added. The research, he said, shows that heat is most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor. “If you’re already in a hot place, the extra couple of degrees are going to be much more dangerous,” he said. Wealthier places, he added, generally have greater access to air conditioning, reliable water supplies and functioning health systems. The study combined seasonal temperature forecasts with localized estimates of how high temperatures affect mortality across more than 24,000 regions worldwide. Researchers estimated the additional heat-related deaths by comparing deaths expected under El Nino-driven high temperatures with deaths expected if temperatures remained similar to what they have been in the last three decades. The projected fatalities are for the entire El Nino period, from June 2026 until the end of February 2027. The report says the Global South will see more heat-related deaths The study by Greenstone and his colleagues also warns that the Global South — a term that isn't geographical but a reference to developing countries in general — will bear the heaviest burden of the excessive heat. The researchers behind the report found that the Sahel region in Africa — countries along the semiarid southern fringe of the Sahara Desert — is expected to be the hardest-hit, with about 66,800 additional deaths caused by El Nino-driven heat. Other major hot spots include South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America, according to the report. The researchers project about 19,400 additional heat-related deaths across the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia, as well as 19,300 in Indonesia, 15,800 in India and 13,300 in Brazil. Heat warnings and cooling centers could prevent thousands of deaths With such staggering numbers, there are recommended measures that governments can take, the report says. They include heat-warning systems, cooling centers, hydration stations, protections for outdoor workers, expanded hospital capacity and targeted outreach to elderly people and other vulnerable groups. The authors also call for what they describe as anticipatory financing, so governments can move resources before dangerous heat peaks. Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the study, said the report’s projections should serve as a call to action rather than be another reason for alarm. But while it's one thing to have well thought-out plans — as India does — implementing these plans and raising needed funds remains a challenge, he said. "The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths,” Tiwari added. Climate change is amplifying El Nino’s record heat El Nino is a natural climate pattern, but this year’s unusually strong event is occurring on a planet already warmed by human-caused climate change, increasing the risks from extreme heat. The Climate Impact Lab said global land temperatures during this El Nino could be higher by about 1.2 Celsius (2.1 Fahrenheit), producing 44% more extremely hot days than in a typical year. The report said those temperature increases may mirror conditions that climate change could make common some 20 years from now. That's why this El Nino could offer a preview of what's ahead as the planet continues to warm, the report said. It's also an opportunity for decision-makers "to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives,” the authors say. ___ The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. item.title: Trump floats banning U.S. diesel exports as prices hit a record $6.52
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump said Tuesday that he would support banning exports of diesel fuel. "I've said let's not send out the diesel," the president said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. "We make a lot of diesel. It could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, you know, it's a sort of a flow. It's a balance." Trump added, "But no, I've called for it. I've called for it within my people. I've been talking about it." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he's examining whether a diesel export ban is feasible, given overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work. The national average price of diesel fuel has surged to an all-time record of $6.52 per gallon, according to AAA , a staggering 77% increase compared to this time last year. Driven primarily by global supply crunches from the wars in Iran and Ukraine, the sudden spike is acting as a massive tax on the US supply chain, which is heavily reliant on diesel to move goods. Because diesel is the economy's primary industrial fuel, its high cost is spilling over into consumer prices nationwide. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, posted on X , "this will backfire and is not good." "U.S. diesel prices are determined not by a U.S. supply and demand balance, but a global one," De Haan wrote. "Keeping distillates and diesel [at] home does not change the world price that reference our prices. You can't fence off a globally traded commodity by executive order and expect the global price to stop applying to it." Economist Joseph Brusuelas warned that the export ban could backfire for another reason: if energy producers pull back on production. The US produces 5.3 million barrels per day, above the 3.6 million barrels of daily domestic demand. He says an export ban would create a short-term domestic surplus, which would then have to be sold at a discount. That, in turn, could cause energy firms to pull back on production, sending prices back up. Jennifer Schonberger is a veteran financial journalist covering markets, the economy, and investing. item.title: Video shows injured man on the ground in Illinois after ICE mistakenly targets U.S. citizen
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A man is recovering from injuries he sustained Sunday morning after ICE officers mistakenly targeted him in a Chicago suburb. In one video verified by NBC News, a Black man is seen sprawled on the street, near a curb, behind a black SUV in Evanston, Illinois. Two agents wearing ICE-style vests are seen standing over him. One of the agents has his face covered and is wearing a vest that reads “POLICE,” and the other appears to be pinning the man down to the ground. The man is shouting at them and can be heard saying, “I’m a f------ U.S. citizen.” According to Evanston police , the man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth, and officers on the scene requested an ambulance. Police said they are investigating the incident, which was recorded by bystanders and gained attention after being posted on social media. One bystander in the background of the video is heard saying the ICE officers used force against the man. Other bystanders begin shouting at the man on the ground, asking him if he is OK. The ICE officers eventually get in the black SUV and drive off, leaving the man on the ground. The bystanders begin trying to help the man and call Evanston police. “I saw two agents pinning down a gentleman. They were using very rough force on him, and it looked like they really did hurt him because we had to call 911,” Miguel Angel Olivares, one of the people who witnessed the encounter, told NBC Chicago on Monday. “When we saw him, he had his jaw swollen and he had a little blood on his shirt. I’m not sure if it was the agent’s or it was his blood,” Olivares said. In a news release Sunday, Evanston police said they spoke to an ICE agent who said federal immigration officers “had attempted to identify an individual who resembled a person they were seeking.” After the man refused to provide identification, he was “detained for fingerprinting, and resisted detention.” An Evanston police officer reported observing blood on the agent’s hands. The agent said he was injured while attempting to handcuff the individual and declined medical treatment, according to the news release from Evanston police. “Agents later determined he was not the person they were seeking and learned that he was a U.S. citizen. He was released.” A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told NBC News in a statement Tuesday that their officers encountered a person who resembled someone they were targeting in an enforcement operation in Evanston on Sunday. “ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement. The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself. ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself,” the DHS statement reads. “DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence.” DHS did not state anything about the injuries the man suffered and why ICE officers did not appear to render aid. Neither the police nor DHS identified the man who was injured. Evanston police said they spoke with the injured man at a local hospital on Sunday. They “photographed and documented his injuries” as part of an ongoing investigation into the incident, police said.
